summary: Defines management objects (a MIB module, NHDP-MIB) for configuring parameters of the Neighborhood Discovery Protocol process on a router. It is a standards-track specification. It was replaced by RFC 7939.

plainLanguage.summary: Routers that find their neighbors need a control panel. This memo defined the dials for it, and later got replaced by a newer panel.

subtitle: Management objects for configuring and monitoring the Neighborhood Discovery Protocol on mobile routers

tldr.problem: The Neighborhood Discovery Protocol (NHDP) allows routers to discover their neighbors in mobile ad hoc networks, but operators need a way to configure NHDP parameters and monitor its performance via SNMP.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6779 defines the NHDP-MIB, a Management Information Base module containing configuration objects, state objects, and performance objects that describe NHDP parameters, current state, and performance metrics.
tldr.outcome: Network administrators can now use standard SNMP tools to configure NHDP, check which neighbors each router has discovered, and gather performance data for troubleshooting. This RFC was superseded by RFC 7939.

today: RFC 6779 was superseded by RFC 7939 in August 2016, which updated the NHDP-MIB to incorporate clarifications and align with subsequent protocol updates. RFC 7939 is the current standard for NHDP management.

sections.title: What NHDP-MIB Provides
sections.content:
RFC 6779 defines the NHDP-MIB, a Management Information Base module for managing the Neighborhood Discovery Protocol (NHDP) defined in RFC 6130. NHDP allows routers in mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs) to discover and track topological information about routers up to two hops away by exchanging HELLO messages.

The NHDP-MIB provides configuration objects to set parameters, state objects to report current state, and performance objects to assess the performance of NHDP. Administrators can use SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) to configure NHDP, check neighbor discovery status, and gather performance metrics for troubleshooting problems and performance issues.
sections.plainLanguage: The NHDP-MIB is like a dashboard in a car. It shows you dials for how often to send neighbor-finding messages, switches to turn the feature on or off, and gauges showing which routers are your neighbors.

sections.title: Structure of the NHDP-MIB
sections.content:
The NHDP-MIB is organized into four main groups:

Configuration Group defines objects that control NHDP behavior: hello message intervals, hold times, jitter limits, and quality thresholds. These are settings an administrator can change to tune protocol behavior.

State Group reports the current operating state of NHDP: which neighbors have been discovered, their addresses, whether links are symmetric, and the state of two-hop neighbors. The state objects reflect the information from RFC 6130's information bases (the local interface set, neighbor information base, and two-hop neighbor information base).

Performance Group provides metrics useful for assessing performance: counters for topology changes, neighbor state changes, and link quality measurements. This helps identify unstable networks or unusual topology changes.

Notifications** (traps) are asynchronous alerts that can be sent when significant events occur, such as a neighbor appearing or disappearing, to avoid flooding the network with polling traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: The NHDP-MIB has four types of controls and readouts: settings you can change, current state information you can read, performance numbers, and alarms for important events.

sections.title: Information Model
sections.content:
The NHDP-MIB structures information around interfaces and neighbors. Each local NHDP interface has its own configuration and state entries. The MIB defines tables to track:

  • Local MANET interfaces on the router and their configuration
  • Local interface network addresses on this router
  • Discovered 1-hop neighbors and their interfaces
  • Discovered 2-hop neighbors and how to reach them
  • Links to neighboring routers (one hop)
  • Performance data for interfaces, discovered interfaces, neighbors, and 2-hop neighbors

Two special data types, NeighborIfIndex and NeighborRouterIndex, map NHDP's dynamic address sets (which define neighbors) to stable indexes suitable for SNMP table indexing.
sections.plainLanguage: The NHDP-MIB keeps separate records for each network interface, each neighbor found, and each two-hop neighbor. It uses index numbers to keep track of them.

sections.title: Configuration and Notifications
sections.content:
Configuration objects include HELLO message intervals (how often to send discovery messages), minimum and maximum intervals, refresh intervals, hold times, and link quality thresholds. These parameters determine how aggressively the router discovers neighbors and how long it remembers them after they stop sending HELLO messages.

The MIB also defines notification (trap) generation mechanisms. Notifications are sent when significant events occur: a neighbor appears, a neighbor disappears, or link state changes. To limit network congestion, the RFC recommends throttling notifications and not sending them during the initial neighbor discovery period. Objects define thresholds and time windows for when notifications should be triggered.
sections.plainLanguage: Configuration objects are like dials for how often to send "hello" messages and how long to remember neighbors. Notifications are alarms that the router can send to a management station when something important changes.

sections.title: Using NHDP-MIB
sections.content:
An SNMP management station can read the configuration group to see current NHDP settings and write to it to adjust parameters. The state group provides a detailed view of the local router's understanding of the MANET: which neighbors it has discovered, which are symmetric (can reach each other), and which 2-hop neighbors it knows about. The performance group provides counters and metrics to help identify network problems, such as frequent neighbor state changes or unstable links.

When a router enables NHDP on an interface (sets nhdpIfStatus to true), it begins sending HELLO messages and discovering neighbors. As neighbors respond, their addresses are recorded in the state group tables. If a neighbor stops sending HELLO messages within the hold time, the neighbor is removed from the tables.
sections.plainLanguage: An operator uses SNMP to turn NHDP on or off, check which neighbors have been found, see performance metrics, and adjust how fast the router looks for neighbors.

sections.title: Security and Management
sections.content:
The NHDP-MIB is a management interface to the NHDP protocol. The security considerations for SNMP apply: access to the MIB objects should be restricted to authorized management stations. Configuration objects are particularly sensitive because changing them affects the protocol's operation. In high-security deployments, an administrator should restrict write access to the configuration group to trusted management stations.

The RFC recommends using SNMP authentication and encryption (SNMPv3) to protect management traffic. Notifications can be sent to multiple management stations, but the rate should be limited to avoid overwhelming the network or management systems during periods of high topology change.
sections.plainLanguage: The NHDP-MIB is a door into the router's neighbor discovery system. Only trusted administrators should have permission to open that door and change settings.
